title: Focal and Ambient Processing of Built Environments: Intellectual and Atmospheric Experiences of Architecture
central_proposition: The human visual system's division into focal (central vision, object-oriented, conscious, intellectual) and ambient (peripheral vision, spatial-oriented, pre-conscious, atmospheric) processing modes fundamentally shapes and differentiates architectural experience.

concept_definitions.name: Central Vision
concept_definitions.definition: The high-resolution visual field extending about 5° from the point of gaze, primarily responsible for detailed object perception.

concept_definitions.name: Peripheral Vision
concept_definitions.definition: The vast remainder of the visual field beyond 5° eccentricity, primarily responsible for spatial perception, motion detection, and scene gist.

concept_definitions.name: Focal Processing
concept_definitions.definition: A mode of visual processing primarily using central vision for conscious, detailed scrutiny of objects and intellectual analysis.

concept_definitions.name: Ambient Processing
concept_definitions.definition: A mode of visual processing primarily using peripheral vision for pre-conscious spatial orientation, navigation, and holistic perception of environmental atmosphere.

concept_definitions.name: Intellectual Experience of Architecture
concept_definitions.definition: Conscious assessment of architectural details and qualities, driven by focal object processing.

concept_definitions.name: Atmospheric Experience of Architecture
concept_definitions.definition: Pre-conscious emotional and mood responses to the overall spatial character of a built environment, driven by ambient spatial processing.

concept_definitions.name: Atmosphere
concept_definitions.definition: The overall emotional impression or mood a person feels in a built environment, influenced by its structure and light, and experienced as a background feeling.

argument_structure: The paper establishes a neurophysiological foundation by reviewing central vs. peripheral vision and their associated visual streams (ventral/dorsal). It then maps these mechanisms to two distinct modes of visual processing—focal and ambient—and argues that these modes give rise to two parallel types of architectural experience: intellectual (conscious, detail-oriented) and atmospheric (pre-conscious, mood-oriented). The argument culminates in proposing empirical tests for these distinctions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is the functional specialization of the visual system: central vision (high acuity, parvo cells, ventral stream) supports focal processing for object recognition and conscious intellectual analysis, while peripheral vision (low acuity, magno cells, dorsal stream) supports ambient processing for spatial perception, navigation, and pre-conscious atmospheric awareness. These two processing modes operate in parallel, with attentional allocation influencing their relative dominance and conscious accessibility.

findings.mechanism: Central vision (fovea) has high cone density, processes fine details, color, form (parvo cells, ventral stream). Peripheral vision has lower cone density, processes motion, spatial relations, scene gist (magno cells, dorsal stream).
findings.source: abstract, The Retina as a Visual Field
findings.quote: Neuroscience has well established that human vision divides into the central and peripheral fields of view.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wilson et al., 1990; Previc, 1998; Strasburger et al., 2011; Whitney and Levi, 2011; Loschky et al., 2017; Siegelbaum and Hudspeth, 2000; Palmer, 1999; Frisby and Stone, 2010.

findings.mechanism: Focal processing (central vision) enables conscious intellectual assessment of architectural details. Ambient processing (peripheral vision) enables pre-conscious experience of architectural atmosphere. These operate in parallel.
findings.quote: We hypothesize that people experience architecture in two basic ways based on these visual limitations; by intellectually assessing architecture consciously through focal object processing and assessing architecture in terms of atmosphere through pre-conscious ambient spatial processing.

findings.consequent: Conscious perception of objects, detailed perception, object recognition, intellectual analysis of architecture
findings.mechanism: High cone density and parvo cell processing in central vision provide high spatial frequencies for perceiving edges and forms, critical for object recognition (Biederman's RBC theory). This is linked to the ventral 'what' pathway.
findings.source: The Retina as a Visual Field, Object Perception
findings.quote: Central vision predominates our conscious vision, and contains what we consider ourselves to be looking at.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Livingstone and Hubel, 1988; Biederman, 1987; Grill-Spector et al., 2001; Larsson and Heeger, 2006; Mishkin et al., 1983; Goodale and Milner, 1992.

findings.consequent: Coarse perception of environment, spatial relations, navigation, scene gist, emotional responses, architectural atmosphere
findings.mechanism: Lower cone density and magno cell processing in peripheral vision are better for detecting motion and larger contrasts (low spatial frequencies), useful for spatial perception and navigation. This is linked to the dorsal 'where' pathway. Crowding effects also limit object recognition in periphery.
findings.source: The Retina as a Visual Field, Object Perception, Scene Perception
findings.quote: The peripheral visual field predominates our pre-conscious vision from which we come to know our visual place in the world.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Leibowitz and Post, 1982; Previc, 1998; Strasburger et al., 2011; Boucart et al., 2016; Ehinger and Rosenholtz, 2016; Larson and Loschky, 2009; Loschky et al., 2015; Eberhardt et al., 2016; Mishkin et al., 1983; Goodale and Milner, 1992.

findings.mechanism: Lower resolution, crowding effects (Bouma's law), and degraded spatial coherence in peripheral vision make object recognition and memory worse.
findings.quote: there is an abundant research showing that object recognition is worse in peripheral vision than central vision
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bouma, 1970; Pelli and Tillman, 2008; Strasburger et al., 2011; Whitney and Levi, 2011; Coy et al., 2014; Geringswald et al., 2016; Velisavljević and Elder, 2008.

findings.antecedent: Semantic inconsistency of objects in a scene (e.g., printer on stove)
findings.mechanism: Peripheral vision is poor at detecting that objects are inconsistent within the rest of the scene; instead, it provides more global characteristics.
findings.quote: when an object seems odd in its surroundings... when viewed with our peripheral vision it does not immediately grab our attention
findings.empirical_support_cited: Võ and Henderson, 2011; Eberhardt et al., 2016; Ehinger and Rosenholtz, 2016.

findings.mechanism: Peripheral vision provides most important information for recognizing scene gist, due to its large visual area and processing of low spatial frequencies (blurry blobs) by M ganglion cells.
findings.quote: the accuracy of scene gist identification with a 5° radius Scotoma was no worse than when seeing the entire scene.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Larson and Loschky, 2009; Loschky et al., 2015; Eberhardt et al., 2016; Schyns and Oliva, 1994; Walther et al., 2009; Arcaro et al., 2009; Baldassano et al., 2016.

findings.mechanism: Central vision is less important for scene gist than peripheral vision.
findings.quote: Conversely, scene gist identification with a 5º radius Window was considerably worse than seeing the entire scene.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Larson and Loschky, 2009; Loschky et al., 2015.

findings.consequent: Spatial orientation, postural control, balance, navigation, pre-conscious awareness
findings.mechanism: Coordination of visual, vestibular, auditory, and somatosensory systems, relying on earth-fixed coordinate systems, optic flow, horizon, linear perspective. Operates pre-consciously.
findings.source: Focal and Ambient Processing and Awareness
findings.quote: the ambient mode is the coordination of our senses, including vision, to aid in determining our place in the world rather than our conscious analysis of it.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Leibowitz and Post, 1982; Previc, 1998; Horrey and Wickens, 2004; Turano et al., 2005; Franchak and Adolph, 2010; Barton et al., 2014; Ehinger and Rosenholtz, 2016.

findings.antecedent: Walking while texting (or similar central vision task)
findings.consequent: Use of ambient vision for navigation (e.g., avoiding obstacles)
findings.mechanism: Ambient vision can handle basic navigation functions even when central vision is occupied, demonstrating its pre-conscious nature.
findings.source: Focal and Ambient Processing and Awareness
findings.quote: it is possible to walk, albeit more slowly and hesitatingly, while texting... it illustrates the use of ambient vision in walking.

findings.antecedent: Driver attention focused on dashboard (focal vision task)
findings.mechanism: Attentional resources are shared between focal and ambient vision, leading to trade-offs. Ambient processing is largely pre-conscious but can be affected by focal load.
findings.quote: drivers can maintain their lane position even when their attention is focused below the dashboard on their radio
findings.empirical_support_cited: Summala et al., 1996; Horrey and Wickens, 2004; Horrey et al., 2006; Ringer et al., 2016.

findings.antecedent: Focal attention (central 20°-30° of upper visual field)
findings.consequent: Conscious awareness of objects, detailed perception, goal-directed processing
findings.mechanism: Relies on eye movements (saccades), retinotopic coordinate system, highly represented in conscious awareness. Adversely affected by low luminance, decreased image quality, lower spatial frequencies.
findings.quote: focal attention plays a critical role in our conscious awareness of objects in our surroundings.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Leibowitz and Post, 1982; Previc, 1998; Horrey and Wickens, 2004.

findings.antecedent: Attending to something covertly (not looking at it) or fixating but not attending/aware
findings.mechanism: Attention is necessary for conscious awareness, but fixation alone is not always sufficient. Peripheral vision contents are often not consciously aware.
findings.quote: we can fail to notice (i.e., be unaware of) something that we are actually looking straight at
findings.empirical_support_cited: Memmert, 2006; Belopolsky et al., 2008; Kuhn and Findlay, 2009.

findings.antecedent: Architectural details (e.g., column rhythms, joinery, edges, vertices)
findings.consequent: Intellectual analysis, aesthetic judgment, focal attention, conscious awareness
findings.mechanism: These features capture focal attention and eye fixations, engaging the ventral 'what' pathway and higher-order cognitive processes like problem-solving and decision-making.
findings.source: Focal Attention and Intellectual Analysis of Architecture
findings.quote: This type of engagement is what aesthetic philosopher Roger Scruton (1979) claims as an intellectual form of judgment about a work of architecture.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Scruton, 1979; Krieger et al., 2000; Mital et al., 2011.

findings.antecedent: Architectural atmosphere (e.g., quality of light, height/width of space, movement of trees, rhythmic patterns)
findings.consequent: Emotional responses, ambient awareness, pre-conscious experience
findings.mechanism: These global spatial features are processed through peripheral vision and the dorsal 'where' pathway, influencing mood and spatial orientation.
findings.source: Ambient Awareness and the Atmosphere of Architecture
findings.quote: The quality of light, the height and width of the space, the movement of trees seen peripherally through the expanse of windows, the rhythmic pattern of frames cascading forward all aid in producing the essential feeling we gain from the atmosphere in the chapel.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Böhme, 2006; Anderson, 2009; Tröndle and Tschacher, 2012; Previc, 1998; Horrey and Wickens, 2004; Foley, 2010.

findings.antecedent: Focusing attention on central vision (e.g., architectural details)
findings.consequent: Overall awareness of the space (ambient processing)
findings.mechanism: Trade-off in attentional resources between focal and ambient processing.
findings.source: Focal Attention and Intellectual Analysis of Architecture
findings.quote: by increasing the number of foveal details to process in an architectural environment, one decreases the viewer's attention to the spatial environment as a whole

findings.consequent: Involuntary capture of attention and eye movements, processing of holistic emotional gist
findings.mechanism: Peripheral vision allows processing of emotional content, even if details are not identified. This emotional gist is hypothesized to be similar to architectural mood/atmosphere.
findings.source: Ambient Awareness and the Atmosphere of Architecture
findings.quote: emotional scenes in the visual periphery can involuntarily capture attention and eye movements... it does allow processing of a holistic emotional gist of a scene
findings.empirical_support_cited: Nummenmaa et al., 2010; McSorley and van Reekum, 2013; Kissler and Keil, 2008; Calvo, 2006; Calvo et al., 2008; Rigoulot et al., 2008.

findings.antecedent: Attentional resources focused in central vision
findings.mechanism: Suggests peripheral visual processing of emotional content requires some allocation of attention, indicating a trade-off.
findings.source: Ambient Awareness and the Atmosphere of Architecture
findings.quote: such emotional processing of peripheral vision is degraded when a person's attentional resources are focused in central vision

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architectural details and qualities will be more frequently described in the window condition (central vision).
Moods or spatial terms will be more frequently described in the scotoma condition (peripheral vision).
Viewers' moods (arousal, valence) will be more influenced by the scotoma condition than the window condition.
Verbal protocols in the control condition (full image) will be more similar to the window condition, while mood measures will be more similar to the scotoma condition.
Hybrid images (details in central, space in periphery) can test the relative influence of central/peripheral regions on verbal protocols and mood measures.
It is possible to recognize architectural mood/atmosphere using only peripheral vision, even when not determined by specific emotionally charged content.
It is possible to perceive architectural mood/atmosphere without paying attention to peripheral vision.
The role of peripheral vision in perceiving architectural mood while navigating through it can be investigated using virtual reality.
bridge_warrants: Connects neurophysiological mechanisms (retina, visual streams) to psychological constructs (attention, awareness, emotion, cognition).
Links aesthetic philosophy (Scruton's intellectual judgment, Böhme's atmosphere) to cognitive science and neuroscience.
Utilizes concepts like gist perception, cognitive maps, attentional allocation, emotional processing, postural control, and interoception.
methodological_critiques: Existing understanding of peripheral visual processing as an essential feature of architectural experience is underdeveloped.
A lack of consideration of ambient processing of architecture has caused trouble in contemporary understanding of architecture.
Over-reliance on regarding architecture only in terms of its focal features, with less regard to its atmosphere perceived through ambient processing.
model_structure: The model proposes a parallel processing architecture where central visual field/focal vision (via parvo cells and ventral stream) is associated with intellectual architectural experience and conscious attention, while peripheral visual field/ambient vision (via magno cells and dorsal stream) is associated with atmospheric awareness and pre-consciousness. This is visually represented in Figure 1, showing the interplay between focal attention and ambient awareness.
limitations: The human visual system is not a strict dichotomy without crossover, but rather a general nature of a divided system.
Neural networks are known to reroute in compensation for lesion damage, potentially providing partially regained perception, even if unconsciously.
The concept of 'architectural atmosphere' is a relatively new theoretical construct in the aesthetics of architecture and geography, requiring further scientific inquiry.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper extends ART by applying its principles of restorative environments to built environments, differentiating how focal and ambient processing might contribute to restoration.
The paper extends SRT by considering how built environments, through focal and ambient processing, might contribute to stress reduction.
The paper assumes the established distinction between focal (central) and ambient (peripheral) visual processing and applies this to how humans perceive and experience built environments.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper proposes that built environment features engage distinct visual processing modes (focal for details, ambient for overall context), which in turn lead to different types of experiences (intellectual or atmospheric).

steps.from_construct: Built environment features (e.g., intricate details vs. overall spatial configuration)
steps.to_construct: Differential engagement of focal vs. ambient visual processing

steps.from_construct: Differential engagement of focal vs. ambient visual processing
steps.to_construct: Distinct intellectual vs. atmospheric experiences of architecture
